Overview

Campus resources at a glance

Electricity, water and waste for eight buildings over 120 days, with the problems the system found and what it recommends doing about them.

What stands out

Five real faults found, each with a cause

A water leak, a broken composter, a dead solar inverter, a library left running on a holiday, and a food-court event surge. Open the Incidents tab for the reasons and actions.

Waste sorting clears the 85% target

The smart-bin classifier reaches 86.3% accuracy in cross-validation and answers in about 33 ms per event.

Demand forecast 7–8% off

Hourly electricity predicted 6 and 12 hours ahead, including through the unseen exam weeks. The Predictive analysis tab lets you enter readings and see what it expects.

Buildings

How the data is fused

  • Hourly meters (23,192 rows): 184 retransmitted duplicates removed on (building, sample hour), keeping the earliest arrival. Rows are ordered by sample time, not arrival time.
  • Offline buildings stay in. The series is re-gridded to 23,040 slots. 101 missing hours (0.4%) are filled from that building's typical load for the same hour and day type, and marked as imputed. 112 rows arrived more than 2 h late (buffer bursts) and are placed at their sample time.
  • Manual logs (415): 38 spellings mapped to 8 buildings; kWh/units, L/kL and kg/bags converted (8 kg per bag). Narrative notes become evidence for incidents.
  • Cross-checks. Hourly sums match the daily summary within 1% on 949 building-days. Manual readings match the meters at a median ratio of 0.99–1.02 by unit (1.08 for bags), with a long tail of outliers that gets flagged, not trusted.
  • Conflict rule. Meter beats manual log; a meter reading that disagrees with a field note about calibration, a stuck meter or a flickering display is quarantined and shown as a data fault rather than as consumption.
  • Dashboard integrity. Late records upsert by (building, sample hour), so a reconnecting building corrects its past without double counting.

Totals use the days with readings; 11 building-days of electricity and water are missing in the daily summary. Cost and CO₂ use the stated constants: Rs 8.00/kWh and 0.70 kg CO₂/kWh.

How accurate the forecast is

Hourly electricity per building. The method was fitted on 20 Jun to 25 Sep and tested on 26 Sep to 17 Oct, a window that includes the whole mid-semester exam period it never saw.

ActualForecast made 6–12 h earlier (chosen method)

Accuracy versus compute

MethodError, 6 hError, 12 hCompute
Same hour last weekNone. A table lookup.
Gradient-boosted trees (lags, calendar, event flag, weather)0.6 s to train; about 0.007 ms per prediction.
Trees blended 50/50 with last weekAs above.
Chosen: typical hour for that building and day type, scaled to the last 6 hoursA lookup and one multiplication. Runs on any edge board and in this page.

Error is weighted absolute percentage error over all building-hours in the test window. The simplest method won, so it is the one used at the edge and in this page, and it needs no model training that could drift. Its profile for exam days is borrowed from weekends in this test, because exams never appeared in the fitting period. The trees used observed weather; a real deployment would use a forecast feed.

Incidents

What went wrong, why, and what to do

Each incident combines a statistical signature with the nearest field note and calendar entry. Real faults rank first, then planned-event surges, then data faults. Value counts electricity at Rs 8/kWh; water counts only pumping energy (0.85 kWh per 1,000 L), because no water tariff was supplied.

Detection rules: robust z-score against the building's own baseline for the same day type, a 01–04 h night-flow rule for leaks, solar below 15% of expectation on a clear day, and composted mass of zero with landfill above 3× normal. Holidays are compared with weekend load, because two holidays are too few samples for a z-score; that is how the B03 holiday load is caught.

Waste classifier

Sorting waste at the bin

Each disposal is identified from five low-cost sensors on the bin itself, so no cloud connection or camera is needed.

F1 by class

Ewaste and glass are the weak classes: both are mistaken for metal and plastic respectively. Plastic and paper confuse each other most in absolute numbers.

What runs on the bin

  • Inputs: the 5 sensors, missing-value flags, log weight, wet weight, hour and building type. Missing readings (about 2%) are handled, not dropped.
  • Model: gradient boosting plus a random forest, averaged. 5.3 MB compressed.
  • Confidence gate: events under 70% confidence are tagged "unsure" and sent to a manual check instead of being counted.
  • Predictions for all 1,601 test events are in waste_events_test_predictions.csv.

Accuracy is from 5-fold stratified cross-validation on the training file with a seed different from the one used for tuning. The test file has no labels, so no test accuracy can be reported. Latency was measured on one CPU thread of the build machine; it has not been run on Raspberry Pi hardware.

Incentives

Rewarding buildings that improve

Credits reward improvement against a building's own baseline, so a big hostel is not punished for being big. Today's standings, computed from the 120 days, are the starting line.

Waste diverted from landfill

Electricity per occupant per day (kWh, lower is better)

How the scoring works

  • Score: each week, the percentage change in kWh per occupant and in diversion rate against the building's own previous 4 same-day-type weeks. Weather and exam days are adjusted by the forecast model, so a heatwave does not cost points.
  • Reward: buildings keep 20% of the Rs 8/kWh they save as green credits (a design assumption), spendable on facilities. The leaderboard also shows a rolling saving in Rs and kg CO₂.
  • Feedback: every Monday each building gets its top two ranked actions from the incident engine, with the reason, in the same view as its score.

How we will know it works

  • Pilot on the two hostels, B05 and B06, which have the same type, composters and similar load per occupant (3.40 and 3.43 kWh). Launch in B05 first; B06 is the control for 6 weeks, then swap.
  • Difference-in-differences on kWh per occupant-day and diversion rate, with the incident days removed.
  • Targets to test, not results: at least 8% lower kWh per occupant and 5 points higher diversion against the control. This dataset has no incentive period, so nothing here is a measured effect.

Cost, scale and risks

What it costs, how it grows, how it can fail

The proof of concept is priced per building, designed to extend from 3 to 30 or more buildings, and checked against three realistic failure modes.

Cost per building

Per-building node (indicative prices, to confirm with suppliers)Rs
Edge computer (Raspberry Pi 4, 2 GB, storage, case)5,500
Energy meter with clamp sensors, water flow sensor, interface boards3,500
4 bin kits (load cell, moisture probe, inductive sensor, photodiode, piezo)5,000
Backup battery, enclosure, cabling2,500
Connectivity and contingency3,500
Budget per building20,000

The budget is the team's stated choice. The dataset has 4 bins per building, which sets the bin-kit line. Inference of 33 ms leaves room for a board much slower than the build machine.

From 3 buildings to 30+

  • All heavy work happens on the building's node: classification, a 12 h forecast and local buffering. The cloud receives one compact row per sample hour and one per classified event, under 100 KB a day for 30 buildings.
  • Every table is keyed by building and sample time, so adding a building adds rows, not schema. Late data upserts on that key and never depends on arrival order.
  • The classifier and the forecaster are one shared model with building as an input, so a new building starts from the shared model and needs about a week of its own data to settle.

Failure modes and fixes

FailureSeen in this dataMitigation
Sensor drift or a bad meterB04 read 6,234 kWh on 27 Aug against about 520 normal while its analyser was being calibrated; B02's water meter read 0 for two days.Cross-check against the hourly sum and field notes; quarantine and impute; never count it as a saving or a spike; monthly meter check against a handheld.
Gaming the incentiveNot observable here. Likely routes: moving waste to another building's bins, mis-sorting to inflate diversion.Score on intensity per occupant against own baseline; low-confidence and high-contamination bins excluded; random audits of 5% of events; a cap on weekly credit gain.
Model decay over a semesterThe forecaster had never seen exam days and was worse than last-week on them (13.6% vs 11.7%).Track weekly error per building; retrain monthly; the blend falls back toward last week when error rises; calendar flags for exams and events feed the model.
